headline: Learn a language, or the owl finds you
copy_notes: Duolingo extended its unhinged-mascot bit — including a staged 'death' of Duo the owl and a cameo-style tie-in around Dua Lipa's album cycle — leaning entirely on organic-feeling stunts rather than traditional media spend. The strategy mirrors the brand's long-running approach of treating its app-store notifications and social account as the actual ad unit.

headline: It's CeraVe. He's Michael Cera. Coincidence?
body_copy: Developed with dermatologists. Also, apparently, with Michael Cera.
copy_notes: CeraVe built a mockumentary-style campaign around the coincidence of Michael Cera's name, running teaser content for weeks before revealing the joke in a Super Bowl spot. It's a rare case of a clinical, dermatologist-endorsed skincare brand using absurdist celebrity comedy instead of the category's usual efficacy-first messaging.

headline: Like a good neighbor, Jake is there
body_copy: Jake from State Farm knows a thing or two, because he's seen a thing or two.
copy_notes: State Farm continued to lean on its 'Jake from State Farm' character, pairing him with athlete cameos across digital cutdowns rather than a single hero spot. The insurer's decade-plus consistency with the same mascot is unusual in a category that typically rotates spokespeople every few years.

headline: Convicted of loving Liquid Death too much
copy_notes: Liquid Death cast real people who had been fired, arrested, or otherwise gotten in trouble for their devotion to the brand, framing canned water with the visual language of a heavy-metal energy drink. The joke only works because the product itself is unglamorous — comedy is doing the differentiation that flavor or price would do for a normal beverage brand.

headline: The soda that loves your gut back
body_copy: Gut health, but make it a soda aisle.
copy_notes: Poppi paired a Super Bowl broadcast spot with a QR-code vending stunt at the stadium, betting that a functional-beverage pitch (prebiotics, low sugar) could work inside a category historically sold on nostalgia and taste. The stunt drew as much commentary for its execution and subsequent backlash as for the ad itself, a reminder that experiential add-ons carry their own reputational risk.

headline: Premium wireless. Shockingly cheap.
body_copy: I own this company. I'm also in the ad. Please buy a plan.
copy_notes: Mint Mobile kept running low-budget-styled Ryan Reynolds cutdowns direct-to-camera, a format built to look inexpensive on purpose — the joke is part of the pitch that the carrier passes savings to customers. The ongoing cadence of short, meme-ready clips is built for the Ad Library format as much as for TV.

headline: The dawn of a new AI
copy_notes: OpenAI's first paid Super Bowl spot leaned on sweeping, humanist imagery rather than a product demo, treating ChatGPT as a moment-of-history event instead of a software feature. It's a notable pivot for a company that grew almost entirely on word-of-mouth and developer buzz, now buying attention alongside legacy consumer brands.

headline: Skip the search. Get the answer.
body_copy: Search, but it actually answers you.
copy_notes: Perplexity's paid social creative positions the product directly against traditional search — screenshots of a cluttered results page next to a clean cited answer — rather than explaining what an 'AI answer engine' is from scratch. The direct-comparison format is a common challenger-brand move: define yourself by what you replace, not what you are.

headline: The card that pays you back
body_copy: 3% back on everything. No categories. No caps.
copy_notes: Robinhood's Gold Card launch ads used a waitlist-and-scarcity framing — a physical card with a visible serial number — to borrow the cachet of exclusive credit products while undercutting them on cash-back terms. The creative deliberately looks like a luxury-card ad, a departure from Robinhood's earlier, more utilitarian trading-app messaging.

headline: Money moves different here
body_copy: Cash Card. Cash Boost. Cash in hand.
copy_notes: Cash App's creative continues to run through artist and creator partnerships rather than product-feature explainers, treating the Cash Card's design drops as a cultural object first and a debit card second. The approach mirrors streetwear marketing more than fintech marketing, which is part of how the brand differentiates from Venmo and Zelle.

headline: Unlock your body's data
body_copy: No screen. No distractions. Just data that matters.
copy_notes: Whoop's ads foreground recovery and strain scores over step counts, targeting a more data-literate fitness audience than the broader wearables market. The subscription-hardware model (the band itself is nominally free with membership) is unusual enough that a chunk of the creative has to do the work of explaining the business model, not just the device.

headline: The tumbler that survived a burning car
body_copy: Built for the wild. Carried everywhere else.
copy_notes: Stanley's marketing largely amplified a customer's own viral video of a Quencher tumbler surviving a car fire with the ice inside still intact, rather than originating the moment itself — the brand's paid media picked up and re-cut existing organic content. It's a case study in a 100-year-old outdoor-gear company repositioning around limited-edition colorways and collector culture instead of durability alone.

headline: This week's flavors are already gone
copy_notes: Crumbl's ads are structured entirely around scarcity and a weekly release cadence, mirroring sneaker-drop marketing more than fast-casual food marketing. The rotating menu gives the brand a reason to post new creative every single week without needing a new campaign concept — the calendar is the campaign.

headline: One scoop, foundational nutrition
copy_notes: AG1 (formerly Athletic Greens) rebranded around the vaguer, more defensible term 'foundational nutrition' rather than specific health claims, a common move for supplement brands navigating regulatory scrutiny. Its ad creative leans heavily on subscription-and-ritual framing — the daily scoop as habit — over any single ingredient story.

headline: Add it to the cart
body_copy: Whatever the recipe calls for, we'll bring it.
copy_notes: Instacart's Super Bowl spot built its visual gag around edible art made from grocery items, a way to make a fundamentally logistics-driven service (delivery, routing, warehouses) feel colorful and food-forward on screen. The category's ads increasingly compete on the emotional register of home cooking rather than convenience or speed alone.
